nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Why retrieval decides the answer § group#0

content.label: Why retrieval decides the answer
content.takeaway: Retrieval quality is paramount for RAG system answer generation.

nodes.title: RAG System Stages
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Why retrieval decides the answer § text#0

content.markdown: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system operates in two stages: first, it retrieves relevant passages from a document collection, and then a language model generates an answer based on those retrieved passages.

nodes.title: Retrieval's Importance
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Why retrieval decides the answer § text#1

content.markdown: The quality of the answer generated by the language model is directly dependent on the quality of the passages provided by the retrieval stage, as the model only has access to these retrieved passages and not the entire document collection.

nodes.title: Harbor Support Assistant Context
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Why retrieval decides the answer § text#2

content.markdown: This document focuses on the retrieval design for the Harbor support assistant, an internal tool that answers questions using approximately 40,000 help-centre articles and release notes.

nodes.title: Takeaway
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Why retrieval decides the answer § text#3

content.markdown: Effective retrieval is crucial for RAG systems, as it directly determines answer quality.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Keyword retrieval with BM25 ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Vector retrieval with embeddings § group#0

content.label: Hybrid Search Components
content.takeaway: Keyword retrieval is precise, vector retrieval is semantic; a hybrid approach is likely best.

nodes.title: Keyword Retrieval (BM25)
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Keyword retrieval with BM25 ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Vector retrieval with embeddings § text#0

content.markdown: Keyword retrieval scores passages based on query terms, weighting rare terms more. BM25 is the standard scoring function, dampening repeated terms and correcting for passage length. It requires no training and is efficient. Its strength lies in exact matching, effectively finding specific codes like `E-4012` or settings like `sync.retry_window` even if they appear rarely. However, it struggles with vocabulary mismatch; for example, "why does my upload stall" won't match "transfers pause when the connection drops".

nodes.title: Vector Retrieval (Embeddings)
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Keyword retrieval with BM25 ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Vector retrieval with embeddings § text#1

content.markdown: Vector retrieval converts queries and passages into numerical embeddings using an encoder model, returning passages with embeddings closest to the query's. This allows matching passages with similar meanings even if they don't share words, enabling a query like "stalled-upload" to find a passage about "paused transfers". However, embeddings are less effective with exact codes and identifiers; `E-4012` and `E-4021` appear similar to the encoder, and rare product names might be fragmented. In tests, vector retrieval alone missed the correct passage for 31 out of 50 error code-centric queries. Embeddings also require recomputation (approximately 6 hours for this collection) whenever the encoder model changes.

nodes.title: Comparison and Implications
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Keyword retrieval with BM25 ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Vector retrieval with embeddings § text#2

content.markdown: Keyword retrieval excels at precise matches for specific terms and codes but fails with semantic variations. Vector retrieval, using embeddings, handles semantic similarity well, overcoming vocabulary mismatch. However, it struggles with the exactness of codes and identifiers, as demonstrated by the high miss rate for error code queries. This suggests that for optimal search performance, especially in technical documentation, a hybrid approach combining both methods would be beneficial to leverage their respective strengths and mitigate their weaknesses.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Combining the two signals ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Candidate generation § group#0

content.label: Combining the two signals
content.takeaway: Hybrid search merges retriever results using RRF to maximize recall.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Combining the two signals ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Candidate generation § shape#0
Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Combining the two signals ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Candidate generation § shape#1
Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Combining the two signals ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Candidate generation § text#0

content.markdown: Hybrid search improves recall when lexical and semantic signals are complementary, meaning each retriever finds unique relevant passages. If retrievers return similar passages or one is poorly tuned, merging adds latency without significant benefit.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Combining the two signals ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Candidate generation § shape#2
Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Combining the two signals ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Candidate generation § text#1

content.markdown:
BM25 scores and vector similarities are on different scales and cannot be directly added. RRF addresses this by using only the rank of each passage.

A passage receives `1/(k + rank)` from each list it appears in, and these contributions are summed. We use `k = 60` (a common default); a larger `k` reduces the difference between top and lower ranks.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Combining the two signals ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Candidate generation § shape#3
Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Combining the two signals ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Candidate generation § text#3

content.markdown:
Each retriever returns its top 50 passages, resulting in a fused list of at most 100 candidates (often fewer due to overlaps).

This stage prioritizes recall over precision; the goal is to include the correct passage, not necessarily to rank it first. Increasing the limit to 100 passages per retriever slightly improved recall but doubled reranking time, so 50 was maintained.

nodes.title: Purpose of Hybrid Search
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Combining the two signals ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Candidate generation § text#5

content.markdown: The sequence aims to combine results from two different retrieval methods (lexical and semantic) to improve the overall recall of relevant passages. This is particularly effective when each retriever finds unique relevant passages.

nodes.title: Merging Mechanism
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Combining the two signals ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Candidate generation § text#6

content.markdown: The core of the merging process is Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). This method is chosen because it normalizes the scores from different retrievers by focusing on rank rather than raw scores, which are on different scales. The `k` parameter (set to 60) influences the weight given to higher-ranked passages.

nodes.title: Candidate List Outcome
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Combining the two signals ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Candidate generation § text#7

content.markdown: Each retriever contributes its top 50 passages. The final candidate list, after fusion, contains at most 100 unique passages. This stage prioritizes recall. The limit of 50 per retriever is a trade-off between recall improvement and reranking time.

nodes.title: Conditional Benefit
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Combining the two signals ⨁ Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Candidate generation § text#8

content.markdown: The effectiveness of hybrid search depends on the complementarity of the retrievers. If both retrievers return similar results, or if one is poorly tuned, the merging process adds latency without significant benefit.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Reranking § group#0

content.label: Reranking
content.takeaway: Reranking improves precision but is limited by initial retrieval and cannot detect outdated information.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Reranking § shape#0
Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Reranking § text#0

content.markdown:
A cross-encoder model is used for reranking. It reads the query and a passage together to output a single relevance score. This method is more accurate than retrievers because it considers both texts simultaneously.

Due to the computational cost, the cross-encoder only operates on the fused candidates, not the entire collection.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Reranking § shape#1
Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Reranking § text#2

content.markdown: Reranking enhances the precision of top results but doesn't guarantee a correct final answer. It can only reorder existing candidates; if the relevant passage isn't retrieved, reranking cannot find it.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Reranking § text#3

content.markdown: A highly relevant passage might be outdated, which relevance scores cannot detect.

nodes.title: Process Overview
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Reranking § text#4

content.markdown: This section describes the reranking process, which involves rescoring fused candidates using a cross-encoder model to improve the precision of the top results. The process is constrained by computational cost and the quality of initial retrieval.

nodes.title: Computational Constraint
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Reranking § text#5

content.markdown: The cross-encoder's high computational cost limits its application to only the fused candidates, not the entire collection. This implies a trade-off between accuracy and efficiency.

nodes.title: Output and Limitations
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Reranking § text#6

content.markdown: The reranking process outputs the top 8 passages. However, it cannot compensate for poor initial retrieval or detect outdated but relevant information, highlighting its inherent limitations.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Generation § group#0

content.label: Generation
content.takeaway: Language model answers questions from provided passages, citing sources, but not their currency.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Generation § shape#0
Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Generation § text#0

content.markdown: The language model receives the user's question and the top 8 relevant passages. It is instructed to formulate an answer *only* using the provided passages and to include citations for each passage used.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Generation § shape#1
Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Generation § text#1

content.markdown: If none of the provided passages contain information relevant to the question, the model is instructed to state this explicitly rather than attempting to answer from its general knowledge.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Generation § shape#2
Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Generation § text#2

content.markdown: The model generates an answer, citing the passages it used. These citations allow readers to verify claims against their source passages. However, citations do not guarantee the currency of the passage content itself.

nodes.title: Example: Error Code Query
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Generation § text#3

content.markdown: For a query like "What does E-4012 mean?", the system retrieves the error-code table via BM25 and a resumable uploads article via vector search. The reranker ensures both are in the top 8 passages, enabling a comprehensive answer that defines the code and explains its fix.

nodes.title: Process Overview
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Generation § text#4

content.markdown: This sequence describes how the language model generates an answer based on retrieved passages. The core achievement is providing a cited answer directly from provided context, preventing hallucination, though it doesn't guarantee source freshness.

nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Relevance, latency and cost § text#3

content.markdown: To meet strict latency budgets, teams can reduce the number of candidates reranked (e.g., top 30 instead of 100), which may impact recall.

nodes.title: Analysis of Search Configurations
nodes.stableKey: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant › Relevance, latency and cost § text#4

content.markdown: The 'Hybrid + reranker' configuration offers the highest relevance (88%) but also incurs the highest latency (190 ms) and cost ($0.95 per 1,000 queries). 'BM25 only' is the most cost-effective and lowest latency option, but with the lowest relevance. The data shows a clear trade-off: higher relevance comes with increased latency and cost. The most notable increase in cost and latency is observed when adding a reranker.
